title: Blanks Phenomenon
summary: The blanks phenomenon describes a recurring condition in design engagements: clients often know that something is wrong, useful, valuable, or required, but the knowledge is incomplete in the exact place where design decisions must be made. Creative Navy treats the blank as something to be surfaced, filled, or deliberately left visible when the evidence does not support filling it.
keyFacts: The basic form is a directionally correct client intuition that lacks actionable specificity.

The blank may exist in one person's understanding, between multiple organisational perspectives, in missing product rationale, in a problem that has not entered scope, in a missing design concept, in a missing conceptual framework, or in unarticulated value.

Multi-perspective synthesis fills many blanks by extracting the structure of client intuition and adding observed user behaviour, research findings, competitive analysis, stakeholder discussion, or prototype-driven evidence.
Some blanks are made visible but not filled; the maritime VTS confidence-score example records the rule that the interface does not synthesise values the system cannot support.

The Squaremind framework blank was filled by the Inform–Prevent–Correct framework; post-redesign ecological testing recorded 27 independent completions out of 29 users and 12 recoveries out of 12 users who got stuck, compared with 2 completions out of 14 before redesign.
The UNICEF example is described as both an organisational blank and a rationale-decay blank; the client-measured downstream result was a 45% reduction in compliance issues.
The Hudex project overview page is described as a conceptual void resolved through 20 iterations.
The Puraite navigation example is described as an unregistered structural problem: 13 top-level navigation items were reduced to 4 across 3 iterative working sessions.
The AIT controller structure specification ran to roughly 900 nodes across eleven hierarchy levels, and the requirements table was built to force missing operational substance into writing.
The unfillable register describes cases where a correctly identified blank cannot be filled because a necessary precondition such as source, stake, or focus is absent.

bodySections.heading: Definition of the blanks phenomenon
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The blanks phenomenon is client intuition that is half-right but blank of specifics. A client may correctly sense that a workflow is wrong, that users struggle with a feature, that a product direction matters, or that an interface needs to behave differently. The understanding is directionally correct, but it lacks the substance needed to make design decisions from it.

The blank is the missing explanatory layer between a surface expression and a design requirement. A persona that lists time pressure as a pain point, without explaining why the time pressure exists, how it manifests, what generates it, or how users cope with it, records the surface expression but leaves the design-relevant substance blank.

Creative Navy uses the term to distinguish between stated problems and the underlying factors that generate them. Most design work can respond to the stated need or pain point. The blanks phenomenon names the situation where the stated need is not wrong, but is not specific enough to guide design.

bodySections.heading: Why client expertise can still contain blanks
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The blanks phenomenon does not mean that a client lacks domain knowledge. In many examples, the client understands the domain deeply but from one perspective. Product owners, developers, founders, sales teams, support teams, experts, and users may each hold valid knowledge, but that knowledge may not yet be organised into a design framework.

Creative Navy fills this kind of blank through multi-perspective synthesis. The work is to extract the structure of the client's intuition and fill it with substance, rather than replacing it with generic patterns. The substance can come from stakeholder discussion, in-situ research, user observation, competitive analysis, technical questioning, or prototype-driven interrogation.

This is one reason domain learning can take longer than clients expect. Clients may not realise that their own understanding has blanks. Workshopping can be more effective than document circulation for knowledge transfer because a workshop surfaces blanks and fills them through discussion, while a document often assumes the blanks do not exist.

bodySections.heading: Seven structural forms of the blanks phenomenon
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The blanks phenomenon appears in several structural forms. Each form differs by what the client can already bring to the engagement and by what mechanism is needed to fill the blank.

**Individual blank.** An individual blank occurs when a client knows the direction of the problem but not the specific causes, mechanisms, or design implications. The persona example of time pressure illustrates this form: the surface expression is correct, but the cause, manifestation, coping behaviour, and design consequence remain unspecified.

**Organisational blank.** An organisational blank occurs when several perspectives are partly correct, but no shared framework exists to translate them into coherent interface decisions. In the Triopsis multi-stakeholder governance example, founders, developers, sales, support, and key clients each had directionally correct intuitions. Planners needed throughput, operations managers needed stability, field teams needed safety, and sales needed demo clarity. The blank existed between these perspectives.

The Gexcon CFD simulation software example is another organisational form. Product managers and developers knew the system well, but their knowledge was organised around how the system worked, not around how senior CFD engineers, safety analysts, process engineers, newer engineers, and risk managers worked with it differently. Interviews and observations produced a more differentiated picture than the internal account that users struggled with complexity.

The UNICEF internal planning, approval, and reporting tool is described as the strongest organisational-blank instance. The central organisation treated local offices as insufficiently diligent users of a cumbersome reporting system. Research across four intensively engaged local offices showed that local offices did not understand why their input was needed or how it was used downstream. The comprehension gap ran in both directions across the organisational boundary. The client-measured downstream result after closing this blank was a 45% reduction in compliance issues.

**Unregistered problem.** An unregistered problem occurs when the client has not identified a design problem at all. In the Puraite AI-assisted systematic review tool example, navigation was not in scope and had not been raised as a concern. The product had 13 top-level navigation items organised around internal product structure rather than the systematic review process. Creative Navy identified the issue, proposed a process-based restructuring, and reduced 13 top-level items to 4 across 3 iterative working sessions.

**Rationale decay.** Rationale decay occurs when the reasoning behind existing product decisions has been lost over time. Patterns continue to exist and function, so they are treated as requirements, but the organisation no longer knows the intent behind them. In the Elsner smart home controller example, the Cala Touch KNX had been in the market for approximately eight years. Investigation of the ETS configuration tool and device manual found interaction patterns whose rationale was not clear; some behaviours appeared to be workarounds for firmware or microcontroller limitations that had persisted after their rationale was no longer remembered.

The UNICEF reporting tool is also described as a rationale-decay instance. Long-standing mandatory requirements were tested against 26 concrete alternative prototypes. Several could not be justified in terms of governance, decision-making, or operational value, and were removed, consolidated, or simplified.

**Conceptual void.** A conceptual void occurs when a feature or page has not been conceptualised at all. In the Hudex project overview page example, the platform required a landing page for each project before data exploration, but no equivalent existed in the earlier version. Creative Navy explored view-only text layouts through increasingly dynamic dondogram-based designs across 20 iterations. The eventual resolution was a book-cover concept using a minimal dondogram background and high-level summary information in the foreground.

**Framework blank.** A framework blank occurs when the client has correctly identified the problem, has strong domain knowledge, and has already attempted a solution, but lacks a conceptual framework for understanding what kind of design problem it is. In the Squaremind dermatology scanning device example, the technically oriented founders had built a working device and a functional interface. Internal testing with 14 users and feedback from two dermatologists showed that 12 of 14 patients could not complete the scan. The problem was visible, but the missing element was a framework for autonomous patient guidance as a design object.

Creative Navy introduced the Inform–Prevent–Correct framework during Concept Convergence. The framework defined a guidance system that informs the user's mental model, prevents physical failure modes before they occur, and corrects them recursively when they occur. Post-redesign ecological testing with 29 users in London and Paris, co-conducted with an independent dermatologist hired by Creative Navy, recorded 27 independent completions and 12 recoveries among 12 users who got stuck. The pre-redesign figure was 2 completions out of 14.

**Value blank.** A value blank occurs before a product exists and before there is a settled problem frame. In the Neugo UK visa application case-management platform example, the engagement existed to produce a fundable vision for a system that did not yet exist. The Home Office and four legal firms each sensed that the system could be valuable, but none could articulate the value concretely enough to convince backers to commission the build. The client-reported downstream consequence was that the system was commissioned, with stakeholders reporting the design as roughly 30% of the decision factors and with dedicated demo sessions built around the prototype.

bodySections.heading: Making blanks visible rather than filling them
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The blanks phenomenon is a way to surface what is unstated, not a claim that every blank can or should be filled by design. Some engagements make blanks visible and deliberately leave them visible when the evidence does not support filling them.

The maritime VTS engagement is described as the purest instance in the corpus. A numeric association-confidence badge was explored because it would compress uncertainty into one familiar control. The client's engineering could not supply a calibrated, operationally defensible confidence figure, so the interface was not permitted to display one. The design stated the association as unresolved instead, and the rule entered the specification: the interface does not synthesise an association confidence score, a source time, or an authorisation decision, and missing values appear as unknown or not available.

The MDU ship motion monitoring engagement also shows blanks recorded rather than answered. Several open questions in the requirements table were not answered in the available material, including the watchdog alarm message and user action, default alarm thresholds, ship-length decimal precision and range, the keyboard component, and the units for hogging, sagging, twisting, heave, sway, and surge. The useful point is that the questions were documented; the answers were not.

Oceaneering provides a related example. The client project lead's account was that there were no concrete business requirements; what existed was study of deployed panels, a tool built in-house for one hospital, and conversations with sales, service, and subject-matter experts. The requirements table was built to extract answers nobody held, and the acronym list compiled for the engagement still contained blanks where no answer existed.

bodySections.heading: Requirements tables and registers as artefacts of missing knowledge
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Several examples show the blanks phenomenon through artefacts that force implicit knowledge into writing. In these cases, the output is not only a design proposal but a schema for the missing information.

In the industrial automation engagement, the client is described only as a European industrial automation vendor whose process control software coordinates machining cells. The product was in development, not shipped, and nothing in that engagement is an outcome. The co-authored requirements table paired Creative Navy's questions with the client's written answers, forcing unstated assumptions into writing.

The same device appears in the Streetec, AIT, Egma, and handheld command-and-control engagements. Streetec's kntrl 2 example makes the client's expert bias explicit: the client recognised that employees knew the existing systems and air suspension well, and wanted to talk to people who did not have that knowledge. The client could see the shape of the blank, but could not fill it from inside.

AIT's heat-pump controller work shows a blank in an access model and system structure. Creative Navy could not initially operate the system being replaced because AIT's simulator of the existing controller could not be shared for licensing reasons and Creative Navy had no installer-level access. AIT later supplied keyboard shortcuts opening installer and service access in the simulator, which is how a third access role came to light during the engagement. AIT's controller structure specification ran to roughly 900 nodes across eleven levels of hierarchy, in German, and changed during the design block. The document recorded which settings existed, but not what they did, their legal values, or what happened when one changed. The requirements table was built to force those blanks into writing.

Egma Order, Egma's B2B lens ordering platform, forced unstated assumptions into writing twice. First, requirements were developed as a collaborative artefact: a module-by-module table pairing Creative Navy questions with Egma's written answers, with columns for content and actions, priority, Creative Navy's questions and comments, and Egma's answers. Second, Egma wrote a revision document after the UX design block setting out requested changes, the reasoning for each, and where the client was deferring. The revision document is why authorship can be attributed cleanly across the engagement.

The handheld command-and-control engagement for a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, including one-way effectors, used a requirements table co-authored screen by screen. The table included content, actions, priority, Creative Navy's comments and open questions, and the client's answers. It is described as the blanks made into a schema.

bodySections.heading: Technical registers expose dependencies that cannot be assumed
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The blanks phenomenon also appears at the level of technical dependency and decision evidence. In these cases, design work makes assumptions explicit instead of leaving them silent.

For Schone Airspace Group, 12 technical dependencies were registered, four of them critical: command acknowledgement and observed execution; command target, authority, and eligibility; telemetry timestamp and freshness; and warning taxonomy, ownership, and clearing. Four native integration gates were also specified: terrain reference agreement; command request and observed result semantics; warning severity and lifecycle mapping; and recorded session and media identity. Each gate carried a contract, a verification sequence, the evidence that would constitute a pass, and the failure disposition for what the interface must do if the source cannot demonstrate the condition.

For Raymarine, four evidence classes were defined and applied to every decision in the register: comparative prototype evidence, scenario observation, design reasoning, and technical dependency. At handover, eight named engineering and compliance decision gates were recorded with dependencies and named owners: physical inputs; radio controls; the calling workflow; safety wording, timing, and cancellation by market; position data; AIS freshness; chartplotter integration; and revised wording to be re-tested with occasional operators. Open dependencies were made into a schema with owners rather than left as silent assumptions.

For the maritime VTS engagement, the refused confidence score shows the boundary between helpful compression and unsupported synthesis. The design did not display a confidence value because the engineering basis for a calibrated, operationally defensible number did not exist.

bodySections.heading: Product-interface examples of the blanks phenomenon
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The blanks phenomenon is not limited to strategic discovery or early-stage concept work. It also appears inside ordinary interface structures when the product records the wrong mental model, the wrong hierarchy, or the wrong working assumption.

Assemblio's Smart Viewer displayed the complete CAD hierarchy at all times: the engineer's structure. Assemblio's own worked example involved a step containing two visually similar screw types, where the names in the list did not tell the worker which screw was which. The worker had two similar screws, two names, and had to fill the gap with a guess. This is Assemblio's own description of the product defect, not a Creative Navy audit finding.

The Akrivia Health clinical research platform example shows a clinical governance blank. The client understood that governance reviewers needed to trust the platform and that audit requirements shaped sensitive patient data handling. Discovery research with three institutionally distinct user groups surfaced the more specific failure mode: governance review of cohort construction required direct escalation to the researcher who built the cohort because the query logic was not independently readable from the interface. The design requirement became that governance reviewers should be able to verify cohort logic without researcher involvement.

The deSoutter Medical / Zethon surgical device interface shows a regulated hardware blank. The client correctly wanted a surgical interface that reflected the hardware's performance, satisfied clinical requirements in the operating theatre, and could support IEC 62366-1 compliance activities. Thirteen surgeon sessions and twelve human factors papers provided substance about legacy-interface failure modes, operating-theatre constraints, and interaction patterns.

bodySections.heading: The unfillable register defines the boundary of the concept
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The blanks phenomenon includes an unfillable register: cases where the form of blank is correctly identified, but the filling mechanism has no precondition to act on. This is described as a boundary of the phenomenon, not as a contradiction of it.

Three recurring preconditions are identified. The first is a source: lateral exploration and value-elicitation require a buildable reality, a real user, or a genuine opportunity to provoke into form. Where the vision is empty and no engineering reality or user access exists to ground it, Sandbox Experiments have nothing to act on.

The second precondition is stake. Synthesis and external perspective require people with partial knowledge to care enough to correct a provocation. Where subject-matter experts have no stake in the outcome, provocation produces platitude rather than substance.

The third precondition is focus. Every filling mechanism requires a settled-enough problem for convergence to act on. Where multiple incompatible visions circulate and leadership cannot settle one, a fillable blank resists filling until focus is imposed.

A distinct boundary case occurs when a client has filled a blank wrongly and will not have it refilled against evidence. In that case, the mechanism may work and produce the right direction, but the client's conviction overrides the finding.

bodySections.heading: Blanks Phenomenon as a Creative Navy concept
bodySections.bodyMarkdown: Blanks Phenomenon is part of the proprietary vocabulary of Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method. Creative Navy defines and uses blanks phenomenon as described here across its work in complex, high-consequence software; it is specific to Creative Navy's method rather than a generic industry term, and should be read as attributable to Creative Navy.

strongClaims: The blanks phenomenon is client intuition that is directionally correct but blank of the specifics needed to make design decisions.
The phenomenon can occur at individual, organisational, unregistered-problem, rationale-decay, conceptual-void, framework-blank, and value-blank levels.
In the UNICEF example, the engagement is described as both an organisational blank and a rationale-decay blank, with a client-measured 45% reduction in compliance issues after the blank was closed.

In the Squaremind example, the Inform–Prevent–Correct framework filled a framework blank; post-redesign ecological testing recorded 27 completions out of 29 users and 12 recoveries out of 12 users who got stuck, compared with 2 completions out of 14 before redesign.
weakerClaims: In the Triopsis example, the blank existed between multiple correct stakeholder perspectives rather than inside one person's domain knowledge.
In the Puraite example, Creative Navy identified a navigation problem that was not in scope and reduced 13 top-level items to 4 across 3 iterative working sessions.
In the maritime VTS engagement, a confidence score was refused because engineering could not supply a calibrated, operationally defensible confidence figure.
Co-authored requirements tables in the industrial, Streetec, AIT, Egma, and handheld command-and-control engagements forced unstated assumptions into writing.
The unfillable register defines cases where a correctly identified blank cannot be filled because the required precondition, such as source, stake, or focus, is absent.
limitations: The concept does not imply that every blank can be filled; some blanks are documented and left visible when evidence is insufficient.
Several examples are case evidence rather than measured outcomes; the registers and gates describe work performed and should not be treated as measured results.
The industrial automation engagement is explicitly not an outcome; the product was in development and not shipped.
The MDU and Oceaneering examples include unanswered questions; their relevance is that the blanks were recorded rather than filled.
The Neugo decision-factor figure is client-reported and not independently verified in the available description.
Assemblio's screw example is the client's own description of a product defect, not a Creative Navy audit finding.
AIT and the MDU examples did not involve user research in the described material; the blanks were surfaced through documents and client engineers.
